rubric.why: Identifies the defining condition for an Arrhenius acid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it dissociates in water. The answer must include both dissociation and water; the product ion is assessed in the next point.

rubric.why: Identifies the ion produced by an Arrhenius acid in water.
rubric.description: It gives a proton or hydronium ion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming either a proton or a hydronium ion.

modelAnswer: An acid is that substance which dissociates in water to give proton (H⁺) or hydronium ion (H₃O⁺).

rubric.why: Identifies the defining condition for an Arrhenius base.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it dissociates in water. The product ion is assessed in the next point.

rubric.why: Identifies the ion produced by an Arrhenius base in water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming hydroxyl ions (OH⁻).

modelAnswer: Similarly, a base is that substance which dissociates in water to give hydroxyl ions (OH⁻).

rubric.why: Defines an acid by its proton-donating role.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying an acid as a proton donor.

rubric.why: Defines a base by its proton-accepting role.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a base as a proton acceptor.

modelAnswer: An acid is a substance that donates a proton.
A base is a substance that accepts a proton.

rubric.why: Names the property that describes water's dual behaviour.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying water as amphoteric.

rubric.why: States the two roles water can perform.
rubric.description: Water can behave as both an acid and a base.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that water behaves as both an acid and a base.

modelAnswer: Water is therefore called an amphoteric compound which means a compound that can behave both as an acid and a base.

rubric.why: Identifies the reacting substances, condition and reaction name.
rubric.description: Acids and bases cancel each other's properties when mixed in equal amounts; this is neutralization.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking an acid and a base mixed in equal amounts with cancellation of their properties or neutralization.
Award 1 mark for naming both salt and water as products.

modelAnswer: Both acids and bases are known to cancel the properties of each other when mixed together in equal amounts. The reaction is called neutralization reaction. A salt and water are formed as a result of this reaction.

rubric.why: Identifies the salt-forming reaction of an acid with a reactive metal.
rubric.description: A reactive metal reacts with an acid to form a salt.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the reaction forms a salt. The example salt MgCl₂ is also acceptable.

rubric.why: Identifies the gas released in the reaction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming hydrogen gas (H₂) as the gas evolved.

modelAnswer: With reactive metals (Mg, Zn) they form salts and evolve hydrogen gas.

rubric.why: Identifies the reaction of acids with metal carbonates or hydrogen carbonates.
rubric.description: Acids decompose metal carbonates or hydrogen carbonates.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the carbonate or hydrogen carbonate decomposes in the reaction.

rubric.why: Identifies the gas evolved in the reaction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming carbon dioxide (CO₂) as the gas evolved.

modelAnswer: They decompose metal carbonates and hydrogen carbonates evolving carbon dioxide gas.

rubric.why: Identifies the reactants in this reaction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an alkali reacts with an ammonium salt.

rubric.why: Identifies the gas released when an alkali reacts with an ammonium salt.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming ammonia (NH₃) as the gas liberated.

modelAnswer: Apart from reacting with acids in neutralization reactions, alkalies also react with ammonium salts and liberate ammonia gas.
